boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Wolgast entry (capitulation, 3 November 1806) in cohort v1's fourth-coalition 1806 group: the Prussian baggage columns of Major Langwerth and Lieutenant Colonel Prittwitz at Wolgast and the French parties that took them, from the arrival of the news of the Anklam capitulation at Wolgast to Langwerth's capitulation, negotiated at Anklam through Count Henckel, and Prittwitz's, signed at Wolgast on 2 November and carried out on the morning of 3 November. The columns' marches, Murat's orders that sent the parties over the Peene and the baggage that had crossed to Usedom are context; the capitulation of the Bila columns at Anklam is a separate entry and is not counted here. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart prints no strength for side A (French), the French under Colonel Daru. He gives side B (Prussian) as 2,500 Prussians, mostly train troops, under Lieutenant Colonel v. Prittwitz and Major v. Langwerth, with 500 wagons and the war chest, whom the French forced to capitulate; the detachment and all its baggage became prisoners of war and the officers were released on parole. By his stated rule his figures are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. Höpfner and the French documents give other accounts (claims side-b-strength, side-b-strength-french, side-a-strength). English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the heading and entry: '1806 3/11. capitulation of Wolgast'; 'the French under Colonel Daru force 2,500 Prussians under Lieutenant Colonel v. Prittwitz and Major v. Langwerth (mostly train troops) with 500 wagons and the war chest to capitulate, after which the detachment with all the baggage became prisoners of war. The officers were released on their word of honour'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian) in Höpfner: two columns. Major Langwerth had left Genthin on 22 October with the baggage of Prince Hohenlohe's troops, escorted in part by a company of the regiment Treuenfels; swollen by all the baggage that had followed from Magdeburg, his column was 500 wagons with 2500–3000 horses by the time it reached Friedland on the 28th. Lieutenant Colonel Prittwitz, the intendant, had left Lindow on the 26th with the army's war chest, the commanders' chaises left behind, pack horses and the sick on requisitioned wagons, escorted by the grenadier battalion Sack and 40 horses, with a crowd of unarmed men. The baggage marched from Anklam for Wolgast covered by the grenadier battalion Sack and a Treuenfels company, which occupied Anklam, with Captain Freyberg of the König von Bayern dragoons forming the outposts; the flour column stayed at Anklam, and General Bila I, arriving there, ordered the grenadier battalion Sack and the Treuenfels company to join his corps. At Wolgast the means of crossing were so poor that only Freyberg's cavalry escort and the baggage of 3 cavalry regiments had crossed when the news of the Anklam capitulation came. Lieutenant Tralles's park column No. 8, which had joined the baggage, burned its vehicles and threw its munitions into the water.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images of pp. 225, 227, 228, 230 and 232, with the end of the sentence on the news from Anklam from the OCR. The columns were brought from the retreat, so the claim is tagged inherited. Höpfner gives no count of the men left at Wolgast. The column had gradually grown very considerably through all the baggage that had left Magdeburg later and followed it, so that the march went forward with extreme difficulty'; 'the company of Treuenfels belonged to the escort of the baggage that had left Genthin under Major Langwerth'; 'on the 27th Neu-Brandenburg was reached, on the 28th Friedland, where the column had reached a strength of 500 wagons with 2500–3000 horses'; 'Lieutenant Colonel and Intendant Prittwitz had, as already related, left the army on the 26th from Lindow with the war chest of the army, the commanders' chaises still left behind, pack horses and the sick carried on requisitioned wagons, under the escort of the grenadier battalion Sack and 40 horses. A crowd of unarmed men had joined him'; 'when General Bila I arrived at Anklam at 10 o'clock in the evening, he ordered that the grenadier battalion Sack and the company of Treuenfels should join his corps'; 'at 10 o'clock in the evening of the 30th the march was begun, covered by the grenadier battalion Sack and a company of Treuenfels, which occupied Anklam, while Captain Freyberg of the König von Bayern dragoons formed the outposts'; 'only the flour column stayed in Anklam, to secure the great need of bread for the troops. claims.value: Side B (Prussian), side A's (French) figures: Déry reported about 2,000 men of all arms at Wolgast, 84 officers and 4,000 to 5,000 horses of dragoons, hussars and caissons, and the capitulation calls the force the garrison of Wolgast, made up of the depots of the regiments of the Prussian army. The report on Captain Guérin's detachment gives 800 men of various cavalry depots of all arms, 1,500 infantry of various corps forming small depots, and 300 caissons or horsed vehicles. Boyer wrote from Anklam that the enemy had only columns of equipages left. Murat wrote from Demmin on 2 November that all the equipages of the army, escorted by about 1,000 men, had passed through the town all the previous day, and that he had sent Déry after them; Belliard reported from Demmin that before the bridge over the Peene was cut many equipages and stray men had crossed into Pomerania, making for Greifswald or Stralsund.
claims.rationale: Side A's figures, read from the page images of pp. 620-621 and 626-628; not reconciled with each other or with Höpfner's and Bodart's (claims side-b-strength, bodart-strength). Höpfner brings Langwerth's and Prittwitz's columns to the Peene by Friedland and Anklam, not by Demmin, so whether Murat's equipages and their escort are the train taken at Wolgast is not shown. The columns were brought from the retreat, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): Déry, 'Chef d'escadron Déry to the Grand Duke of Berg. Wolgast, 2 November 1806'; 'I have the honour to send you herewith the capitulation made between Lieutenant Colonel de Prittwitz and me. There are at this'; 'moment at Wolgast about 2,000 men of all arms, 84 officers and 4,000 to 5,000 horses of dragoons, hussars and caissons. The King's treasure of 10 millions had already gone off 6 days ago by Anklam. I found at Wolgast only one regimental chest containing 1,000 francs in small change'; the capitulation, '1. Capitulation of the garrison of Wolgast between the lieutenant colonel and intendant M. de Prittwitz and M. Déry, lieutenant colonel, aide-de-camp of His Imperial Highness the Grand Duke of Berg'; 'Art. 1. The garrison of Wolgast, made up of the depots of the regiments of the Prussian army, is prisoner of war; it will march out of the place tomorrow at 9 o'clock, lay down its arms on the glacis and hand over all the horses, wagons and other effects belonging to His Majesty the King of Prussia'; '2. The officers of the different regiments will keep their arms,'; 'horses and baggage; they will pledge their word of honour not to serve against His Majesty the Emperor and King until duly exchanged; they will receive passports to return to their homes. The footmen will return home'; '3. All the chests of the regiments, those belonging to the King and those that may be on the island of Usedom will be faithfully handed over'; 'done at Wolgast, 2 November. Prittwitz. Déry'; the report, 'report of the detachment of Captain Guérin, of the 10th dragoons, which left Demmin on 2 November with 50 men of the regiment and 50 men of the 11th'; 'this detachment left Demmin at 2 o'clock in the morning, made for Wolgast (Swedish Pomerania), marching in pursuit of the baggage of the Prussian army'; 'the detachment arrived near Wolgast at nightfall, fell on the enemy outposts and took them prisoner; as soon as the outposts had been carried, Captain Guérin sent M. Coulon, sub-lieutenant of the regiment, with a trumpeter to summon'; 'the enemy corps to surrender. This summons was accepted; 800 men of various cavalry depots of all arms, 1,500 infantry of various corps, forming small depots, and 300 caissons or horsed vehicles were the result of this affair'; 'Colonel Dommanget, of the 10th dragoons'; Boyer, 'Chef d'escadron Boyer to General Belliard. Anklam, 2 November 1806'; 'I am going to cross into Sweden with 25 men to reconnoitre the march of the enemy, who, according to the information I have, is passing onto the island of Usedom, chiefly by Wolgast; but he has only columns of equipages left, to which I have had Major Langvert tell them that I granted them the same capitulation as him. They will arrive tomorrow; but, General, please give me orders about these horses and baggage'; Murat, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor. Demmin, 2 November 1806, 10 o'clock in the morning'; 'there passed through this town yesterday, all day long, all the equipages of the army escorted by about 1,000 men; I have sent after them my aide-de-camp Déry with 1 squadron of dragoons by the bridge of Demmin, and 1 squadron of hussars by Jarmen toward Gützkow to take them in flank, while my squadron of dragoons will stop their head at Anklam. The first convoy having capitulated this night at Anklam, I have reason to think that everything that has crossed the Peene will capitulate likewise'; Belliard, 'General Belliard to the Major General. Demmin, 1 November 1806, 9 o'clock in the morning'; 'the bridge over the Peene had been cut; before it was broken many equipages and stray men had crossed into Pomerania, following the Peene and making for Greifswald or Stralsund;'; 'it appears that the Swedes will not let them pass, for a convoy of equipages escorted by various detachments has sent 2 officers by Anklam to capitulate, which was done in the night'; 'this morning 3 squadrons crossed the Peene at Demmin, Jarmen and Anklam to set off in pursuit of all the detachments and baggage that threw themselves into Pomerania yesterday,'; footnote 1, 'this report bears as its date in the register 1 November, 9 o'clock in the morning. It is entered in the middle of the correspondence of 2 November. It is probable that it was begun on the evening of the 1st and finished only on the 2nd at 9 o'clock in the morning, from the phrase This morning 3 squadrons.... It should be dated at the head Demmin, 1 November, and at the foot, 2 November, 9 o'clock in the morning'.

claims.value: Side A (French): Bodart names the French under Colonel Daru and gives no strength. Höpfner: a French raiding party under Colonel Darü approached Wolgast. Murat wrote to the Emperor from Demmin on 2 November that he had sent his aide-de-camp Déry after the Prussian equipages with 1 squadron of dragoons by the bridge of Demmin and 1 squadron of hussars by Jarmen toward Gützkow, to take them in flank, while his squadron of dragoons stopped their head at Anklam. In the Prince's name Belliard ordered Lasalle to send a squadron of his brigade over the Peene at Jarmen toward Gützkow, adding that 2 squadrons of dragoons were crossing at Demmin and Anklam, and told Boyer that a squadron of hussars was crossing at Jarmen and one of dragoons at Demmin; his report to the Major General has 3 squadrons crossing the Peene at Demmin, Jarmen and Anklam. Déry wrote from Wolgast that he would leave 50 men from the 2 detachments of dragoons and hussars to escort the captured train and rejoin Murat with the rest of his troop; a note gives these as a dragoon detachment from Demmin and a hussar detachment from Jarmen. The report on Captain Guérin's dragoon detachment has it leave Demmin with 50 men of the 10th dragoons and 50 of the 11th. No passage read gives the strength of the hussar squadron, so no total for side A is given.
claims.rationale: Bodart, Höpfner and the French documents, read from the page images; the letters of pp. 618-621 were read as this battle's targeted follow-up, the note on p. 627 referring to p. 618. Guérin's detachment numbers 100 men (our arithmetic). The squadron at Anklam is not counted here. A remark printed after Déry's letter says that he does not mention the detachments with him and that Guérin does not appear to have been under his orders (claim side-a-command). English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; Höpfner, 'meanwhile an enemy raiding party under Colonel Darü approached the town of Wolgast. Lieutenant Colonel Prittwitz, who had meanwhile also arrived from Usedom, was summoned to surrender by a parlementaire'; Murat, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor. Demmin, 2 November 1806, 10 o'clock in the morning'; 'there passed through this town yesterday, all day long, all the equipages of the army escorted by about 1,000 men; I have sent after them my aide-de-camp Déry with 1 squadron of dragoons by the bridge of Demmin, and 1 squadron of hussars by Jarmen toward Gützkow to take them in flank, while my squadron of dragoons will stop their head at Anklam. The first convoy having capitulated this night at Anklam, I have reason to think that everything that has crossed the Peene will capitulate likewise'; Belliard, 'General Belliard to General Lasalle. Demmin, 2 November 1806, half past six in the morning'; 'the Prince orders you to have a squadron of your brigade cross the Peene at Jarmen to make for Gützkow, which appears to be the route the equipages of the Prussian army have followed; cross at Demmin; you will stop everything you can find, and the Prince orders that all the chests be kept intact (the same order as for chef d'escadron Boyer)'; 'the squadron that crosses the Peene may fall back on Anklam or on Demmin as circumstances allow; 2 squadrons of dragoons are crossing the Peene at Demmin and at Anklam to scour the country'; 'General Belliard to chef d'escadron Boyer, at Anklam. claims.value: Höpfner: Count Bronikowski (claim side-b-command) had already given the officer of the 22nd dragoon regiment commanding at Anklam such an account of the column's state that Count Henckel, on his arrival, could only conclude a capitulation for Langwerth's column, by which the escort laid down its arms as prisoners of war, the officers, NCOs and men kept their property, royal property was handed over, and nothing more might cross the Peene after 6 in the afternoon of 1 November. Meanwhile a French raiding party under Colonel Darü approached Wolgast and summoned Prittwitz by a parlementaire, demanding all the chests and the property of the absent officers; the latter demand was dropped. Foucart prints Boyer's letter from Anklam of 2 November, saying that he had had Major Langwerth tell the remaining columns of equipages that he granted them the same capitulation; Déry's letter from Wolgast sending Murat the capitulation made between Prittwitz and himself; and the report on Captain Guérin's detachment, which left Demmin at 2 in the morning in pursuit of the Prussian baggage, fell on the enemy outposts at nightfall and took them, and sent Sub-Lieutenant Coulon with a trumpeter to summon the enemy, which accepted. A remark printed after Déry's letter says that Déry does not mention the detachments with him and that Guérin does not appear to have been under his orders.
claims.rationale: Höpfner and the French documents, read from the page images. The summonses and terms were the French officers' own steps at Anklam and Wolgast; Murat's orders that sent the parties are in claim posture. claims.value: Höpfner: Major Langwerth, without news of the army since the 26th and without further orders, decided at Friedland to take the road to Anklam. Prittwitz and Langwerth went ahead to Usedom to arrange supply and the crossing; Prittwitz fell mortally ill there, and Langwerth, given bad horses at the Amt Pudagta (as printed), reached Wolgast only on 1 November. When the news of the Anklam capitulation came, insubordination spread and the column dissolved; when the major came back (by the context Langwerth; the OCR line that names him is garbled) the idea of capitulating arose and many officers joined in; Rittmeister Count Henckel, who was against it, let himself be persuaded to negotiate with the French general at Anklam, and on seeing that the enemy had not yet entered Swedish territory sent Lieutenant Schmeling back to Langwerth to protest once more; but Lieutenant Count Bronikowski, who had pushed himself in as a companion, galloped into Anklam ahead of him (OCR passages) and gave the officer of the 22nd dragoon regiment commanding there such an account of the column's state that Henckel could only conclude a capitulation for Langwerth's column, not naming Prittwitz's. Höpfner notes that Bronikowski soon after entered the service of the Polish insurgents. Langwerth went to Anklam himself to get better terms. Prittwitz, summoned at Wolgast, tried in vain to separate the royal from the regimental chests and, once the demand for the absent officers' property was dropped, concluded a second capitulation that gave up the regimental chests too; it was carried out on the morning of 3 November. Höpfner finds no excuse for Langwerth's conduct but the complete exhaustion of all strength, which produced a state that excluded any vigorous measure (OCR passage for the end of the sentence); otherwise the chests could have been taken over the Peene, the horses swum across, the rest destroyed and the men ferried over by force (OCR passage).
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images of pp. 228, 230 and 232, with the OCR passages marked. Höpfner does not name his sources for this passage. English renderings (ours): 'at Friedland Major Langwerth received the news that the enemy was already raiding as far as Pasewalk, news that an officer sent out confirmed. As the major had learned nothing of the army since the 26th and had received no further orders, he decided to take the road to Anklam'; 'Lieutenant Colonel Prittwitz and Major Langwerth went ahead to Usedom to make arrangements for supply and for ferrying over the Peene. The lieutenant colonel was struck down at Usedom by a mortal illness, and Major Langwerth, at the Amt Pudagta, where he had arranged everything with the officials, was given such bad horses that he could reach Wolgast only on 1 November'; 'the baggage had arrived safely, but the means of crossing at Wolgast were so meagre that only the cavalry escort of Captain Freyberg and the baggage of 3 cavalry regiments had been ferried over when the news of the'; 'capitulation at Anklam arrived' (OCR); 'insubordination spread, and the news spread by soldiers coming back that Swinemünde too was already occupied by the French brought about a complete dissolution' (OCR); 'but when that major came back, the thought of capitulation arose with him, and many of the officers present joined in. Count Henckel was against it, but at last let himself be persuaded to undertake the negotiation and to travel to Anklam, to arrange what was necessary with the French general there' (OCR); 'but when the Rittmeister perceived that the enemy had not yet set foot on Swedish territory at all, he sent Lieutenant Schmeling, who was accompanying him, back to Major Langwerth to make representations against the capitulation once more' (OCR); 'the other accompanying officer, who had pushed himself into this company, a Lieutenant Count Bronikowski of the Henckel cuirassiers, was to wait for Rittmeister Count Henckel at the junction of the roads to Anklam, but instead rode into Anklam at a gallop' (OCR); 'to keep him from a rash step, but came too late'; as in claim side-a-command for Bronikowski's account and the terms; 'he soon afterwards went into the service of the Polish insurgents'; 'Major Langwerth went to Anklam himself to obtain better terms'; 'meanwhile an enemy raiding party under Colonel Darü approached the town of Wolgast. Lieutenant Colonel Prittwitz, who had meanwhile also arrived from Usedom, was summoned to surrender by a parlementaire'; 'he tried in vain to make the Frenchman understand the difference between royal and regimental chests; the delivery of all chests was demanded, as well as the property of the absent officers'; 'as at last at least the latter demand was dropped, Lieutenant Colonel Prittwitz had to resolve to conclude a second capitulation, which thus differed from the first in that the regimental chests too were handed over. It was carried out on the morning of 3 November'; 'there is no other excuse for the conduct of Major Langwerth than the complete exhaustion of all strength,'; 'by which a state was produced that excluded any vigorous measure' (OCR); 'otherwise the simplest thing would have been: to get the chests over the Peene, have the horses still strong enough swim across, burn and smash everything that could not be saved, have the men present ferried over by the Wolgast boatmen under compulsion, and then sink all the boats' (OCR).

claims.value: Bodart records the capitulation of Wolgast on 3 November: the French under Colonel Daru forced 2,500 Prussians under Prittwitz and Langwerth, with 500 wagons and the war chest, to capitulate; the detachment with all its baggage became prisoners of war and the officers were released on parole. Höpfner heads his passage 'capitulation of Wolgast on 2 and 3 November': Langwerth's column capitulated through Count Henckel at Anklam, and Prittwitz concluded a second capitulation at Wolgast, carried out on the morning of 3 November. On the French side Belliard reported that a convoy of equipages escorted by various detachments had sent 2 officers by Anklam to capitulate, which was done in the night, and Murat wrote on 2 November that the first convoy had capitulated that night at Anklam. The capitulation Foucart prints, signed at Wolgast on 2 November by Prittwitz and Déry, makes the garrison of Wolgast prisoners of war, to march out of the place the next day at 9, lay down its arms on the glacis and hand over the King of Prussia's horses, wagons and effects; the officers keep their arms, horses and baggage and give their parole not to serve until exchanged; the footmen go home; and all the regimental and royal chests, including those on Usedom, are to be handed over.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome with Höpfner's account and the capitulation, read from the page images; no source read gives a different result. Bodart's date is the day Höpfner has the second capitulation carried out. Neither Belliard nor Murat names the convoy that capitulated by way of Anklam, so that it was Langwerth's column is not shown; footnote 1 to Belliard's report judges the report begun on the evening of the 1st and finished on the 2nd, so which night it means is not shown either. claims.value: Bodart places Wolgast, a town in Pomerania, at the mouth of the Peene, opposite the island of Usedom; his locator names the country as Prussia and does not say whether it describes 1806. The report on Guérin's detachment places Wolgast in Swedish Pomerania, and Höpfner has the baggage cross the Peene onto Swedish territory, where Swedish officers would allow only transit through Swedish Pomerania. Murat wrote of the squadron of dragoons pursuing the baggage on the left bank of the Peene in Swedish Pomerania, and Belliard told Boyer not to begin hostilities with the Swedes but to reply if they opposed his march. The means of crossing at Wolgast were meagre (Höpfner; claim means-and-supply). The capitulation has the garrison march out of the place and lay down its arms on the glacis. Those who got across went on over Usedom to Swinemünde (OCR passage).

claims.value: Boyer wrote from Anklam on 2 November that by his information the enemy was passing onto the island of Usedom, chiefly by Wolgast, but had only columns of equipages left, and that he would cross into Sweden with 25 men to reconnoitre. Guérin's detachment marched from Demmin in pursuit of the Prussian army's baggage. Déry reported the force and the single chest he found at Wolgast and that the King's treasure had gone by Anklam 6 days before; a remark printed after his letter says he did not mention the detachments with him. Murat reported that all the equipages of the army had passed through Demmin all the previous day with an escort of about 1,000 men; Belliard took Gützkow to be the route the Prussian equipages had followed, and reported that the Swedes appeared not to be letting them pass. Höpfner says Count Bronikowski gave the officer of the 22nd dragoon regiment commanding at Anklam an account of the column's state (claim side-b-command).
claims.rationale: The French documents and Höpfner, read from the page images. English renderings (ours): Boyer, 'Chef d'escadron Boyer to General Belliard. They will arrive tomorrow; but, General, please give me orders about these horses and baggage'; the report, as in claim side-b-strength-french; Déry, 'Chef d'escadron Déry to the Grand Duke of Berg. Wolgast, 2 November 1806'; 'I have the honour to send you herewith the capitulation made between Lieutenant Colonel de Prittwitz and me. There are at this'; 'moment at Wolgast about 2,000 men of all arms, 84 officers and 4,000 to 5,000 horses of dragoons, hussars and caissons. The King's treasure of 10 millions had already gone off 6 days ago by Anklam. I found at Wolgast only one regimental chest containing 1,000 francs in small change'; the remark, as in claim side-a-command; Murat and Belliard's report, as in claim side-b-strength-french; Belliard's order to Lasalle, as in claim side-a-strength; Höpfner, as in claim side-a-command.

claims.value: Side A (French) attacked: Murat sent his aide-de-camp Déry with a squadron of dragoons by Demmin and a squadron of hussars by Jarmen after the Prussian equipages that had passed through Demmin, and Belliard, in the Prince's name, ordered the Jarmen squadron to stop everything it could find (Foucart). A French raiding party approached Wolgast and summoned Prittwitz by a parlementaire (Höpfner); Guérin's detachment, pursuing the baggage, fell on the outposts at nightfall, took them prisoner and summoned the enemy, which accepted (the French report). Side B's outposts, surprised, could not resist, and Langwerth's column capitulated at Anklam through Count Henckel without fighting.
claims.rationale: Coded A_attacked: side A advanced on and summoned side B, which capitulated. open_questions: Deferred: a French return of the prisoners, horses, wagons and chests; the strength of the hussar squadron sent by Jarmen; the text of Langwerth's capitulation beyond Höpfner's summary; the records of the Prussian judicial inquiries held after the war, on which by the preface of his first volume Höpfner's work chiefly rests; whether Höpfner's Colonel Darü and Bodart's Colonel Daru are Foucart's Déry, Murat's aide-de-camp, who signed the capitulation with Prittwitz at Wolgast (the party, place and date agree, the names and ranks do not); where the wagons of flour, grain and baggage that Belliard reports taken in the night were taken (Foucart t. II, p. 620), which are not assigned to this entry. Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated: the hour at which the war chest left Anklam for Usedom, the day of the column's rest at Anklam and the length of the joined columns (Höpfner, p. 229), and a figure in the garbled OCR line on how the war chests went on from Kolberg to Danzig (p. 233).

Most consequential gap: the size of each side at Wolgast. The targeted follow-up read the order to which the note on Foucart t. II, p. 627 refers and the French letters around it (pp. 618-621): side A was Déry with a squadron of dragoons and a squadron of hussars, the dragoon detachment 50 men from each of its two regiments by the report, but no passage read gives the hussars' strength. Side B's figures (Bodart's 2,500 mostly train troops with 500 wagons; Höpfner's 500 wagons and 2500–3000 horses for Langwerth's column at Friedland; Déry's about 2,000 men, 84 officers and 4,000 to 5,000 horses; the report's 800 cavalry depot men, 1,500 infantry and 300 vehicles; Murat's escort of about 1,000 men for the equipages that passed Demmin) are not reconciled, and none says how many came under Langwerth's capitulation and how many under Prittwitz's. A French return of the prisoners could settle side B.

Disputes kept as separate claims: the strength (as above); the war chest (taken, Bodart; embarked at Anklam on the 29th, Höpfner, with the war chests reaching Kolberg by Wollin in his OCR passage; the King's treasure of 10 millions gone off by Anklam 6 days before Déry's letter of 2 November and a single regimental chest of 1,000 francs found, Déry); the French commander (Colonel Daru, Bodart; Colonel Darü's raiding party, Höpfner; Déry, chef d'escadron in the heading of his letter, lieutenant colonel and aide-de-camp of the Grand Duke of Berg in the capitulation and Murat's aide-de-camp in Murat's letter, who signed the capitulation, with Guérin's detachment apparently not under his orders by the remark printed after his letter, Foucart); one capitulation (Bodart) or two (Langwerth's at Anklam and Prittwitz's at Wolgast, Höpfner, with Boyer's grant of Langwerth's terms to the columns of equipages and Belliard's and Murat's convoy that capitulated by way of Anklam in the night); the date (3 November, Bodart; 2 and 3 November, Höpfner; signed on 2 November to be carried out the next day, the capitulation); the town's country (Prussia, Bodart's locator, which does not say whether it describes 1806; Swedish Pomerania, the French report, Murat and Höpfner's Swedish officers); the fortification code (B_fortified on the capitulation's 'place' and 'glacis'; none_named on every other passage read).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his sources for this entry were not checked, though his 500 wagons match Höpfner's, his 2,500 men equal the lower of Höpfner's figures for the column's horses, 2500–3000, and his Colonel Daru matches Höpfner's Colonel Darü); Foucart, t. II (the French side's documents: Murat's letter to the Emperor, Belliard's orders and report, Boyer's and Déry's letters, the capitulation and Colonel Dommanget's report on Guérin's detachment, all from the page images); Höpfner, Bd. 2, 2nd edition (the Prussian side's history; by the preface of his first volume the work rests chiefly on the records of the judicial inquiries held after the war, but the Wolgast passage names no source).
